courses.description: This course introduces the fundamental concepts of machine learning and artificial intelligence, covering key algorithms and models.
courses.enrollment_requirement: For students in MSc Artificial Intelligence for Science
courses.learning_outcomes: By the end of Foundations of Machine Learning and AI, students will understand basic machine learning ideas, e.g. linear regression and classification in terms of loss, likelihood, and decision theory, and explain the architecture of deep neural networks, training via gradient descent and backpropagation. Students will be able to discuss the roles of regularization, convolutional neural networks, autoencoders, and attention/transformers at a conceptual level.
courses.course_syllabus: This course covers foundational concepts underpinning machine learning and AI. Following a brief review on linear algebra, probability and information theory for ML, various learning models and training will be covered, including single-layer regression/classification, loss/likelihood and MLE, least-squares geometry, bias–variance, discriminant functions/decision theory, and optimization via (stochastic) gradient descent and backpropagation with regularization (weight decay, dropout, learning curves). Selected topics (instructor-added) may include CNNs, autoencoders, and transformers/attention.

courses.description: Students will learn essential programming skills using Python, focusing on problem-solving and data analysis techniques applicable to AI.
courses.enrollment_requirement: For students in MSc Artificial Intelligence for Science
courses.learning_outcomes:
By the end of this course, students should be able to:

* write Python code beyond “notebook hacking”
* clean messy data, run analyses, and produce figures
* build reusable modules/classes for research tasks
* handle errors properly (not crash silently)
* create reproducible environments that others can run
* collaborate professionally with Git/GitHub
* run a baseline machine learning workflow using scikit-learn

Specifically, the students can aim to achieve the following objectives:

A. Core Python Programming Competence

* Write correct Python programs using variables, expressions, control flow, loops, and functions to solve data-driven problems.
* Use Python data structures effectively (lists, tuples, dictionaries, sets) and apply common patterns such as slicing, iteration, list comprehensions, and functional tools (e.g., zip, enumerate, lambda).
* Work confidently with strings and encodings, including text processing tasks commonly encountered in scientific data and AI pipelines.

B. Software Design and Object-Oriented Programming

* Apply object-oriented programming (OOP) principles—inheritance, encapsulation, abstraction, and polymorphism—to build modular and reusable code.
* Design basic Python modules and scripts, separating logic into functions/classes and structuring code for clarity and maintainability.

C. Practical Engineering Skills for Reliable Coding

* Debug and interpret Python errors, using error messages, print-based inspection, and systematic debugging strategies to identify and fix issues efficiently.
* Implement robust programs with error handling, including exceptions, input validation, and defensive coding practices.

D. Data Handling and Scientific Computing

* Read, write, and manage files and datasets, including common formats (CSV/JSON/TXT), using appropriate File I/O techniques.
* Use NumPy for numerical computing, including array operations, vector/matrix/tensor manipulation, and efficient computation through vectorization.
* Use pandas for data extraction, cleaning, transformation, and aggregation, preparing datasets for downstream analysis and modelling.

E. Visualization and Communication

* Create clear and informative visualizations using Matplotlib, selecting appropriate chart types and formatting to communicate results effectively.

F. Reproducible and Collaborative Workflows

* Build reproducible Python environments using conda/mamba, manage dependencies, and control randomness using seeds.
* Collaborate using Git/GitHub, including basic version control operations, branching workflows, pull requests, and code review practices.

G. Quality Assurance and Maintainability

* Improve reliability and code quality using assertions, logging, basic testing (pytest), and (introductory) type hints to support correctness and future extension.

H. Applied AI Programming (Tool-Oriented, Not Theory-Heavy)

* Use common ML/AI Python libraries as practical tools (e.g., scikit-learn and introductory exposure to TensorFlow/PyTorch/Keras) to: a) load and preprocess data, b) train baseline models, c) evaluate performance using standard metrics, and d) run simple end-to-end modelling workflows.
courses.course_syllabus:
The course syllabus ensures that all students develop:

* Python programming skills for AI applications
* Practical data analysis and visualization abilities
* Foundational knowledge of linear algebra and calculus as applied in AI
* Hands-on experience in building and deploying machine learning models for real-world problems

1) Python Fundamentals for AI Programming

* Fundamental concepts

* Python syntax and execution model (script vs notebook)
* Variables, expressions, operators, statements
* Data types (int/float/bool/None), type conversion
* Control flow: conditionals and loops
* Functions: parameters, return values, scope
* Pythonic iteration: zip, enumerate, list comprehensions, basic lambda

What is covered

* Writing correct programs to solve small computational problems
* Basic algorithmic thinking and code structure

Not covered (in depth)

* Advanced algorithm design / competitive programming

2) Data Structures and Text Handling

* Fundamental concepts
* Core containers: lists, tuples, dicts, sets
* Indexing, slicing, mutability vs immutability
* String processing: formatting, splitting, parsing
* Encodings and Unicode awareness (UTF-8, common pitfalls in scientific text data)

What is covered

* Practical manipulation of structured data (tables, mappings, records)
* Text processing typical in logs, datasets, metadata, and scientific outputs

Not covered (in depth)

* Formal language processing or NLP models

3) Object-Oriented Programming (OOP) for Reusable Code

* Fundamental concepts
* Classes/objects, methods, attributes
* Encapsulation and abstraction (API design mindset)
* Inheritance and polymorphism (when/how to use them)
* Code organization into modules

What is covered

* Building simple, reusable components for scientific/AI workflows

Not covered (in depth)

* Design patterns at enterprise-level complexity

4) Input/Output, File Processing, Libraries, and Error Handling

* Fundamental concepts
* File I/O: reading/writing text and structured formats (CSV/JSON)
* Import system and modular scripts
* Standard library vs third-party libraries
* Exceptions, try/except, defensive programming, user input validation

What is covered

* Building robust scripts that work on real datasets and files

Not covered (in depth)

* Systems programming, OS internals

5) Reproducible Computing and Collaborative Development

* Fundamental concepts
* Environment management: conda/mamba, dependency specification
* Reproducibility principles: versions, fixed seeds, deterministic workflows (as feasible)
* Git/GitHub essentials: commits, branches, pull requests, code reviews

What is covered

* Creating research-ready code that others can run and verify

Not covered (in depth)

* Large-scale DevOps/CI pipelines (may be briefly introduced as optional)

6) Numerical Computing and Data Analysis

* Fundamental concepts
* NumPy arrays: shape, dtype, broadcasting, vectorization
* Matrix/tensor operations and efficient computation
* pandas DataFrames: indexing, filtering, merge/join, groupby, missing values
* Data cleaning and transformation pipelines

What is covered

* Preparing and transforming datasets for analysis/modelling

Not covered (in depth)

* Advanced statistical inference (handled in Mathematics & Statistics for AI)

7) Scientific Visualization

* Fundamental concepts
* Plot selection for different data types (trend, distribution, comparison)
* Basic Matplotlib usage and good plotting practices
* Interpreting visual results and communicating findings

What is covered

* Producing figures for reports and research presentations

Not covered (in depth)

* Interactive dashboards and advanced visualization libraries (optional extension)

courses.description: This course provides a solid foundation in the mathematical and statistical concepts necessary for understanding and developing AI models, including linear algebra, probability, and statistical inference.
courses.enrollment_requirement: For students in MSc Artificial Intelligence for Science
courses.learning_outcomes: Students completing this course gain the mathematical foundations needed to understand, design, and build AI models. They use linear algebra (vectors, matrices, eigenvalues, SVD) to structure data and representations; apply multivariate calculus and computation graphs to derive and implement backpropagation; and wield probability, information theory, and inference to formulate principled objectives (entropy, cross‑entropy, KL). They diagnose conditioning and stability, choose effective SGD/optimizer strategies, and reason about constraints. They reduce dimensionality with PCA, model latent structure via GMM/EM, and leverage the mathematics of CNNs for vision. The result is a disciplined ability to translate real problems into robust, well‑optimized AI systems.
courses.course_syllabus:
Core Content:

Linear algebra

* Vectors, matrices, tensors
* Matrix operations, dot product, norms
* Linear independence, span, rank, eigenvalues, SVD

Calculus & computation graphs

* Gradients, Jacobians, Hessians
* Multivariate chain rule
* Computation graphs

Probability and information theory

* Random variables, PDFs/PMFs
* Joint, marginal, conditional probability
* Expectation, variance, covariance
* Entropy, cross‑entropy, KL divergence

Statistical inference

* Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE)
* Maximum a Posteriori (MAP) and Bayesian inference
* Least Squares, Mean Squared Error (MSE), logistic regression
* Bias–variance trade‑off

Optimization

* Gradient descent, convexity, constrained optimization
* Condition number, stability, step size
* Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD), momentum, RMSProp, Adam
* Line search & curvature considerations

Dimensionality Reduction

* PCA via eigenvalues and SVD
* Probabilistic PCA
* Applications to preprocessing, compression, visualization

Latent Variable and Mixture Models

* Gaussian Mixture Models (GMM)
* Expectation–Maximization (EM)

Selected Content:

Probabilistic Generative Models

* Likelihood‑based generative models
* Conceptual introduction to VAEs and GANs
* ELBO and variational inference at a high level

Bayesian Networks and Graphical Models

* DAG structure, factorization
* Conditional independence; inference
* Learning graph models conceptually

courses.description: This course explores the transformative applications of AI in research, innovation, and technology across various science disciplines. Through engaging case studies and practical examples, students will discover how AI is reshaping the landscape of modern science and technology. Students will attend lectures featuring different science researchers, who will share how AI has been utilised in their fields. Designed to be accessible, the course emphasizes the practical applications of AI in science without requiring advanced programming skills or in-depth knowledge of AI techniques.
courses.enrollment_requirement: For students in MSc Artificial Intelligence for Science
courses.learning_outcomes: By the end of this course, students will be able to explain how AI is being applied across a range of science disciplines and describe the opportunities and limitations these applications create for research and innovation. They will be able to interpret and discuss real-world case studies presented by researchers, identifying the research questions addressed, the types of data involved, and the role AI plays in generating or validating insights. Students will also be able to outline the history and motivation behind these problems, including why they matter scientifically and how approaches have evolved over time.
courses.course_syllabus: Core topics cover major AI applications in the sciences, organized around a rotating set of researcher-led talks and case studies. Each talk introduces an applied scientific problem and the AI approach used to address it, without assuming advanced programming. Across the series, students engage with examples from multiple science domains (as determined by the invited speakers) and develop a shared foundation in discussing AI-enabled research in context. The course also includes dedicated weeks for student presentations, where students synthesize one talk/theme, communicate key ideas to peers, and connect it to broader scientific motivation and context. Specific talk topics may change each year.

courses.description: This course is designed for students with foundational science or computational backgrounds seeking to understand how artificial intelligence (AI) transforms life sciences research and applications. No prior experience in life sciences is required. The course aims to provide essential biological principles to AI-driven solutions across five interconnected domains: macromolecular structure determination, cell imaging, bioinformatics, drug discovery, and personalized medicine and nutrition. Students will learn how AI addresses key technical challenges—from protein folding and genomic analysis to clinical trial optimization—while developing competency in interpreting AI outputs in biological contexts. By course completion, students will understand both the capabilities and limitations of AI applications in advancing life science research.
courses.enrollment_requirement: For students in MSc Artificial Intelligence for Science
courses.learning_outcomes: Students will understand how artificial intelligence (AI) addresses fundamental challenges across the life sciences—from protein folding and cell imaging to genomic analysis, drug discovery, and personalized medicine. They will compare classical and AI-based approaches, interpret AI outputs in biological contexts, and critically evaluate the impact of AI on accelerating scientific discovery while engaging with ethical considerations required for responsible AI development in life science applications.
courses.course_syllabus: This course explores how AI addresses fundamental challenges across five interconnected domains of life science research. Module 1 covers macromolecular structure—from structural biology fundamentals to AI-driven protein folding and de novo design. Module 2 examines cell imaging, focusing on microscopy principles and how AI facilitates overcoming challenges in cellular microscopy imaging such as noise, resolution, and annotation. Module 3 addresses real-world applications in personalized medicine and nutrition, grounded in ethical frameworks and stakeholder engagement. Module 4 introduces bioinformatics, comparing classical pipelines with AI approaches for genomic and transcriptomic analysis, emphasizing biological data interpretation. Module 5 traces AI's integration throughout drug discovery—from target identification to clinical trial design and optimization. From the modules, students will be able to develop competency in translating AI capabilities to assist in tackling issues in life research endeavors and applications

courses.description: This course focuses on how artificial intelligence is applied specifically to chemical data and chemical discovery workflows. Building on machine learning concepts covered in the core modules, students will learn chemistry-aware representations (e.g., molecular graphs and 3D conformations), data curation and evaluation strategies (e.g., scaffold splits, dataset bias, uncertainty), and practical modelling pipelines for molecules, reactions, and spectroscopy. Through case studies and hands-on exercises using Python and chemistry toolkits such as RDKit (and modern deep learning frameworks), students will develop the ability to design reliable AI workflows for real chemical problems including molecular property prediction, reaction outcome modelling, catalyst screening, and data-driven discovery. The course features an invited seminar session delivered by a guest speaker. Students will undertake an individual or group project and give a presentation in the final week.
courses.enrollment_requirement: For students in MSc Artificial Intelligence for Science
courses.learning_outcomes:
1. **Describe** the unique characteristics and challenges of chemical data that influence how AI methods are applied in chemistry.
2. **Recognise and use** common chemistry representations (e.g., SMILES, molecular graphs, basic 3D conformations) and apply standard preprocessing and data curation practices.
3. **Apply** chemistry-aware evaluation strategies (e.g., scaffold splitting) and **identify** common issues such as data leakage, dataset bias, and uncertainty in model predictions.
4. **Interpret and compare** representative AI approaches for key chemistry tasks (e.g., molecular property prediction, reaction prediction/retrosynthesis, and molecule generation) using case studies and guided exercises.
5. **Complete** a small-scale individual or group project that applies course concepts to a chemistry dataset, and **communicate** the main results and limitations in a final presentation.
courses.course_syllabus: Core topics include: (1) unique characteristics of chemical data and why chemistry AI differs from generic ML; (2) chemistry-aware representations and preprocessing (SMILES, molecular graphs, basic 3D conformations, data curation/standardisation); (3) reliable evaluation in chemistry (scaffold-based splitting, data leakage, dataset bias, and uncertainty awareness); (4) representative AI approaches and case studies for molecular property prediction, reaction prediction/retrosynthesis, and constraint-aware molecular generation; and (5) guided hands-on exercises and a small-scale project with final presentation, with optional enrichment via an invited research seminar.
